\section{Overview} \label{sec:Overview}
Go is a programming language that concurrently executes lightweight threads, called goroutines, with shared memory.
A goroutine is a sequentially executing program that expresses an order on lines of code \parencite{go/ref/mem}.

We consider Go programs that execute on distributed systems.
According to \textcite[Chapter 4]{vanSteen2017distsys}:
\begin{quote}
  a distributed system is a concurrently executing collection of autonomous computing elements. Each computing element is called a node. Since nodes are autonomous, we cannot always assume that there is a global clock that synchronizes the actions of all nodes. The nodes:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item are geographically dispersed, so that sending and receiving takes a long time, and may be arbitrarily delayed.
  \item can join and leave the system, and the connection network between nodes continuously changes topology and performance.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{quote}

The goal of this work is to describe a verification framework that can verify that an implementation satisfies a specification.
Users of our framework should follow the following software development methodology:
A specification designer writes a specification that the programmer's Go implementation is supposed to satisfy.
A programmer writes a distributed Go implementation.
If our framework then verifies that the implementation does not satisfy the specification, then both the programmer and the specification designer should rewrite their implementation and specification.
On the other hand, if our framework then verifies that the implementation satisfies the specification, then users of our framework can be confident that the implementation always has properties that the specification guarantees, no matter what kind of interleaving execution the implementation can have.

\subsection{Basics}
\textcite{Kurose1999ComputerN} gives the following informal dentition of protocols: ``a communication protocol defines the format and the order of messages exchanged between two or more communicating entities''.
In this work, the informal definition is made formal to have an unambiguous meaning, in order to for it to guide how we structure our verification framework:

\begin{definition}
  For distributed Go programs, specifications are global protocols.
\end{definition}

Furthermore, we say that a distributed Go program satisfies a global protocol if it communicates according to the protocol.
The notion of global protocols is formalized in section \ref{sec:Global Protocols}.

We now define ``parties'', the interacting elements of a concurrent system.
A party is a goroutine that has some line of code that is either a send or receive.
Parties are denoted in general by $\Party$. When referring to specific parties, we use the notation that ranges over $\{\party{A}, \party{B}, \party{C}, \party{D}, \ldots\}$.

Events are denoted in general by $\E{i}$, where $i$ is an index. Where an event belongs to party $\Party$, we use $\Ep{\Party}{i}$, where $i$ is an index.
Two events $\E{}$, $\E{'}$ may be ordered by a happens-before order, denoted by $\E{} \HB{} \E{'}$.
Our happens-before order $\HB{}$ order differs from Lamport's happens-before order \parencite{lamport1978time}, details deferred to section \ref{sec:HB Order}.

Figure \ref{fig:control flow and events} shows one party that has one event.
The figure looks like a sequence diagram that has only one participant: the lifeline is vertical, and time flows downwards.

\input{figures/control_flow_and_events.tex}

We focus on applying our framework to verify that a Go program is communication race-free, for the first in, first out (FIFO) communication model.
In this work, we do not mention data races, except in reference to other works. Therefore, mentions of races refer only to communication races.
A usual definition of FIFO ordering in distributed systems is given by \textcite[Section 12.1]{Garg2004ConcurrentAD}, as follows:
\begin{quote}
  We use $e \prec f$ to denote that $e$ occured before $f$ in the same process.
  Let $s_1$ and $s_2$ be any two send events and $r_1$ and $r_2$ be the corresponding receive events. Then FIFO ordered computations is defined as $s_1 \prec s_2 \implies \neg(r_2 \prec r_1)$.
\end{quote}
This usual definition assumes that channels are not shared: if two processes are connected by a channel, then the channel connects only these two processes \parencite[Section 7.2]{Garg2004ConcurrentAD}.

However, this assumption is not valid in Go.
In Go, concurrently executing goroutines can access the same shared memory, as well as communicate with other concurrently executing goroutines over FIFO channels.
The sharing of a channel with concurrently executing goroutines presents a new problem not considered by the usual definition of FIFO ordering: despite the FIFO property of channels, it is possible that the messages sent end up at unexpectedly different receiving goroutines.
For example, even if a programmer writes the program \ref{lst:simple global protocol implementation} expecting \lstinline{B} to receive \lstinline{1} and \lstinline{C} to receive \lstinline{2}, this may not actually happen.
The program may execute with races, because communication does not proceed as specified by the global protocol designer.
It is possible for \lstinline{C} to receive \lstinline{1} and \lstinline{B} to not receive anything at all, because channel \lstinline{c} is shared between the goroutines that run \lstinline{go A()}, \lstinline{go B()}, and \lstinline{go C()}.

\input{lstlistings/simple_global_protocol_implementation.tex}

The invalid assumption of the usual definition of FIFO ordering motivates a different-than-usual definition of FIFO ordering of events for the Go programming language: we need to extend FIFO ordering to many concurrently executing goroutines.
Details in section \ref{sec:Transforming Global Protocols with Races into Race-free Global Protocols}.

\subsection{Transforming Global Protocols so that Satisfying Implementations are FIFO Race-free}
We call implementations that never execute with a race ``race-free implementations''.
On the other hand, we call implementations that may execute with a race ``implementations with races''.
If a global protocol may be satisfied by an implementation which may execute with races, then we call this a ``global protocol with races''.
Otherwise, we call this a ``race-free global protocol''.

Figure \ref{fig:satisfaction with and without races} describes how global protocol designers can use our framework to convert a protocol with races to a race-free protocol, and how these protocols relate to implementations that a programmer writes.
The figure shows only the implementations that our verification framework can verify with success.

\input{figures/satisfaction_with_and_without_races.tex}

Our framework can verify that implementation \ref{lst:simple global protocol implementation} satisfies the following global protocol, where two transmissions are sequentially composed, and each transmission is of the form $\transmit{\Party}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'}$ (read as ``the $i^{th}$ transmission of the protocol specifies that party $\Party$ sends a message to party $\Party'$ over channel $\Channel$'', or ``the protocol specifies that event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ sends a message to the receive event $\Ep{\Party'}{i}$ over channel $\Channel$''):
\input{subequations/global_protocol_with_races.tex}
However, our framework cannot guarantee that the implementation \ref{lst:simple global protocol implementation} is race-free, because the global protocol \eqref{eq:global protocol with races} does not conditionally guarantee the property of race-freedom.

Global protocols conditionally guarantee race-freedom by having certain guards at certain positions in the global protocol.
A guard $\guardP{\E{} \HB{} \E{'}}$ is an abstraction over how its happens-before element $\E{} \HB{} \E{'}$ is proven to be in the $\HB{}$ order.
Race-freedom is guaranteed on the condition that if verification of an implementation against that global protocol succeeds, then the verification shows that the implementation is race-free.

For example, the global protocol \eqref{eq:global protocol race-free} conditionally guarantees race-freedom, by having two guards in between its two transmissions.\footnote{If the guards were not there, these transmissions may race.}
\input{subequations/global_protocol_race-free.tex}

As figure \ref{fig:satisfaction with and without races} shows, the race-free global protocol \eqref{eq:global protocol race-free} was obtained by applying the transformation described in section \ref{sec:Transforming Global Protocols with Races into Race-free Global Protocols} on the protocol with races \eqref{eq:global protocol with races}.
If users of our framework correct the original implementation with races to become a race-free implementation \ref{lst:simple global protocol guarded implementation}, then as shown by figure \ref{fig:satisfaction with and without races}, our framework can verify that this corrected implementation satisfies the race-free global protocol \eqref{eq:global protocol race-free}.

\input{lstlistings/simple_global_protocol_guarded_implementation.tex}

Indeed, the verification shows that the implementation is race-free, because the implementation \ref{lst:simple global protocol guarded implementation} transmits between $\party{A}$ and $\party{B}$ on an unbuffered channel $\channel{d}{0}$ to order the events $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$, and transmits between $\party{B}$ and $\party{C}$ on an unbuffered channel $\channel{e}{0}$ to order the events $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}$.
Therefore, the implementation \ref{lst:simple global protocol guarded implementation} used two extra transmissions to fix a linear order of send events and a linear order of receive events.
These orderings are sufficient for the implementation to always execute such that $\party{B}$ receives data from $\party{A}$, and $\party{C}$ receives data from $\party{B}$, because Go channels are FIFO.
This means all executions of the implementation satisfy global protocol \eqref{eq:global protocol with races}, such that the implementation satisfies the global protocol.
In other words, the implementation always communicates according to the protocol: the implementation transmits according to $\transmit{\party{A}}{\Channel}{1}{\party{B}}$, then transmits according to $\transmit{\party{B}}{\Channel}{2}{\party{C}}$, and the implementation can never transmit in any other way.
Furthermore, the implementation also satisfies global protocol \eqref{eq:global protocol race-free}, because the two guard orders have been proven.

\subsection{Details of Verification}
In this work, we restrict how a Go program can be verified as race-free: Go programs must use Go's synchronization primitives to be verified as race-free.
Although Go's sync package \parencite{go/pkg/sync} defines many kinds of synchronization primitives, we require race-free Go programs to order their transmissions by synchronizing goroutines on an unbuffered channel.
We call such a synchronizing transmission on an unbuffered channel a ``rendezvous'' between the send and the receive of the transmission.
This restriction of synchronization to rendezvous simplifies verification, because the rendezvous is specified by the happens-before order over unbuffered channels, and our verification framework already models the happens-before order over unbuffered channels.

Although the given global protocol offers a global view of the communication, we opt for a modular verification where each channel endpoint in each party may be independently verified.
This means that verification can be parallelized.
To this purpose, the global protocol is projected onto parties, and then projected again onto channel endpoints.
Our framework then deductively verifies by using Hoare triples to consume the heads of each endpoint's protocol.
The verification succeeds, because the implementation has rendezvous on channels \lstinline{d} and \lstinline{e}.
Each rendezvous forces all events before the rendezvous to happen-before all events after the rendezvous, even if these events occur in different parties.
Therefore, the parties in the implementation must communicate in a race-free way.

\subsection{Channels in the Go Programming Language}
Go channels are FIFO: if there is an $i^{th}$ send and $i^{th}$ receive on the channel, then the $i^{th}$ receive on the channel receives data from the $i^{th}$ send on the channel. If there is no $i^{th}$ send on the channel, the $i^{th}$ receive blocks until there is an $i^{th}$ send on the channel.

A channel variable can be in shared memory, and accessed by concurrently executing goroutines.
We emphasize that despite the FIFO property of channels, a program may still send messages to unexpectedly different receiving parties.

Go channels are typed, and all messages on a channel must type check against the channel type. This may lead to runtime type errors if the channel type is something like a sum type, discussion of which is deferred to section \ref{sec:Avoid Runtime Type Errors}.
For brevity, in the rest of this work, unless necessary, we do not mention channel types, message types, and message values.
We still mention them in Go programs, because they are used by the Go compiler.
We also mention message values when we use the extended per-endpoint protocol syntax \ref{lst:extended per-endpoint protocol syntax}.

A channel buffer stores the messages provided by sends on the channel, that have not yet been received.
Channel buffers have a nonnegative size and a nonnegative capacity.
The size of a channel is the number of messages currently stored on the buffer.
The capacity of a channel is the number of messages that can be stored on the buffer, before the buffer is full.
A channel with nonnegative capacity $k$ is denoted by $\channel{c}{k}$.
An ``unbuffered channel'' is a channel with zero capacity, denoted by $\channel{c}{0}$.
A ``buffered channel'' is a channel with positive capacity, denoted by $\channel{c}{k}$ for some positive $k$.
If we do not care about the capacity of channel, we denote the channel by $\Channel$.
In this work, channels range over $\{\channel{c}{k}, \channel{d}{k'}, \channel{e}{k''}, \channel{f}{k'''}, \ldots\}$, for some nonnegative $k, k', k'', k'''$.

\section{Program Order, Events, Sequential Consistency, and Parties} \label{sec:Program Order, Events, Sequential Consistency, and Parties}
To ease our analysis, similar to the approach of \textcite{ng2016deadlock}, we convert a Go program to its Single Static Assignment (SSA) representation \parencite{go/tools/ssa}. Then we represent a goroutine as a control flow graph (CFG), where nodes are blocks of a Go program, and directed edges are the ordering of events given by program order.
We show only some graphs in table \ref{tab:control flow representation}, other graphs are defined as usual and not shown.

\input{tables/control_flow_representation.tex}

Inside each block of code, control flows sequentially from one line of code to another.
For each line of code, we abstract away all information except the duration during which program control flows through the line of code. This information is called an ``event''.
We use the terminology in figure \ref{fig:start completion terminology} to refer to parts of an event.
\input{figures/start_completion_terminology.tex}
This terminology is adopted from \textcite{fava2020ready} where they rephrased the send and receive rules of the memory model of Go.
The rules of Go's memory model are restated in figure \ref{fig:send receive rules}.

Not only does $\HB{}$ relate events in program order, it also relates sends and receives according to the memory model of Go, given by rules \eqref{eq:send before receive} and \eqref{eq:receive before send}.

\input{figures/send_receive_rules.tex}

Rule \eqref{eq:send before receive} says that a receive must wait for some data to be written by a send, before it begins receiving data.
Note that the time at which the receive starts may be earlier than the time at which the receive begins receiving data. In this case, during the time in between, the receive blocks as in execution \ref{fig:rendezvous with blocked receive execution}.

Rule \eqref{eq:receive before send} says that if a channel buffer is full with $k$ messages, then a receive must begin receiving data from the channel so that the buffer is not full anymore, before a send begins sending data.
Note that the time at which the send starts may be earlier than the time at which the send begins sending data. In this case, during the time in between, the send blocks as in execution \ref{fig:rendezvous with blocked send execution}.

\input{figures/rendezvous_with_blocked_send_and_blocked_receive_executions.tex}

Parties are the interacting elements of a concurrent system.
A party is a goroutine that has some line of code that is either a send or receive.
It is not necessary for a goroutine to be a party.
For example, in program \ref{lst:simple global protocol implementation}, goroutines \lstinline{A}, \lstinline{B}, and \lstinline{C} are parties.
Even though the CFG of the goroutine \lstinline{main} has directed edges to the CFGs of \lstinline{A}, \lstinline{B}, and \lstinline{C} as indicated by the keyword \lstinline{go} (the CFG of goroutines with keyword \lstinline{go} was shown \hyperlink{cfg:go}{in this cell} in table \ref{tab:control flow representation}), \lstinline{main} does not have any line of code that is either a send or receive.
Therefore \lstinline{main} is not a party.
For the rest of this work, \lstinline{main} is never a party.

We want to show executions in the form of sequence diagrams, for better explanation.
However, the memory model of Go says:
\begin{weak} \label{weak:reorder}
The execution order observed by one goroutine may differ from the execution order observed by another goroutine.
\end{weak}
Therefore, it seems that for a single execution with $N$ goroutines, we need to show $N$ sequence diagrams, each as observed by one of the goroutines.
Despite this, only one sequence diagram is enough.
This is because sends and receives of one goroutine cannot be observed to execute differently by another goroutine.
Therefore, it is enough to consider only the execution where each goroutine sees itself executing according to its program order, and all other goroutines also see that this goroutine executes according to the same order.
In other words, it is enough to show only one order of events (the program order) on each lifeline in a sequence diagram.

An execution may be shown as a sequence diagram with many goroutines.
Each goroutine has a lifeline.
Events of each goroutine happen on the lifeline, and happen in program order.
All events happen at a specific time on the global clock, along a specific horizontal line in the sequence diagram.
This explains why the executions of Go programs are sequentially consistent if the Go programs have only sends and receives.

According to \textcite{10.1007/978-3-319-95582-7_15}, for a memory model \textit{inspired} by Go, executions of Go programs are sequentially consistent under data-race freedom (up to when an execution has a data race).
We believe this claim of sequential consistency also holds for the memory model of Go, for executions up to when the execution has a communication race.

\section{$\HB{}$ Order} \label{sec:HB Order}
We define our $\HB{}$ order by taking inspiration from Lamport's happens-before order.
Program order as mentioned in section \ref{sec:Program Order, Events, Sequential Consistency, and Parties} is a subset of $\HB{}$.
Events not ordered by $\HB{}$ may either happen in either order, or may happen at the same time.

However, in our work, we do not take inspiration from Lamport's other ideas. This simplifies our approach.
For example, although Lamport's happens-before order is related to Lamport's thread-local clocks, we do not define any local clocks.
Therefore, our approach is simplified because we do not have to synchronize any clocks.
In other words, we assume all events happen relative to the same global clock.
Although this assumption appears to contradict the characteristic of distributed systems that nodes are autonomous, this is assumption is sound in our work, because we focus only on verifying FIFO race-freedom.
To verify, we only need to prove that sends on one endpoint of a shared channel are ordered by $\HB{}$, and that receives on the other endpoint of the same shared channel are ordered by $\HB{}$.
It is reasonable to assume that events occuring on an endpoint happen relative to the same global clock.

Our $\HB{}$ order differs from Lamport's happens-before order \parencite{lamport1978time}.

Lamport's events happen instantaneously, whereas we use the terminology \ref{fig:start completion terminology} to refer to the start and completion of events with duration, in the same way that Gischer's tasks \parencite{gischer1988pomsets} happen over a duration.\footnote{Unlike Gischer's tasks, our events are unique, therefore we do not need a multiset of events; a set is enough.}

Lamport's happens-before order is a strict partial order over a set of events (irreflexive and transitive, therefore also asymmetric), whereas our happens-before order is also a strict partial order, but over a set containing both their starts and their completions. We must distinguish between the start of an event and its completion so that we can describe the events of a rendezvous with a $\HB{}$ order.

\subsection{Rendezvous} \label{sec:Rendezvous}
Recall the two rules \eqref{eq:send before receive} and \eqref{eq:receive before send} relating sends and receives.
The two rules allow for the send to start sending data at the same time that the receive starts receiving data (assuming a channel with no propogation delay). Similarly, the two rules allow for the send to complete sending data at the same time that the receive completes sending data.
Therefore, an unbuffered channel can be modelled by the two rules.
To apply rule \eqref{eq:receive before send} on unbuffered channels, we say that an unbuffered channel has capacity $0$.

A transmission on an unbuffered channel executes as in the rendezvous execution \ref{fig:rendezvous with duration execution}.
The rendezvous execution \ref{fig:rendezvous with duration execution} shows that there must be an overlap between the duration during which the send happens, and the duration during which the receive happens. The actual transmission happens instantaneously at some point during the overlapped durations. This corresponds to our intuitive notion of unbuffered channels: both the sender as well as the receiver must be ready to send and ready to receive, before the transmission can happen.
This assumes no propogation delay, because if the propogation delay is significant enough, then the completion of the send can happen-before the receive.
Significant propogation delay conflicts with the definition that the actual transmission happens instantaneously at some point during the overlapped durations.

We now compare how our $\HB{}$ order differs from Lamport's happens-before order, when representing a rendezvous.

\begin{enumerate}
\item By Lamport's definition, $\HB{}$ cannot contain both $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{\channel{c}{0}} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ and $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ because $\HB{}$ is asymmetric. The execution \ref{fig:rendezvous without duration execution} captures this notion. Note that the two arrows corresponding to $\HB{}$ are horizontal arrows,\footnote{The arrows are horizontal if we require that all arrows are straight. Even though the arrows in the figure have been curved so that it is easier to tell them apart, we still consider these arrows to be horizontal.} indicating that $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ and $\Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ happen-at the same time.
\item By our definition, $\HB{}$ can contain both $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{\channel{c}{0}} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ and $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{A}}{1}$, because the $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ in $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{\channel{c}{0}} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ refers to the start of the send event, whereas the $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ in $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ refers to the completion of the send event. This does not violate asymmetry, since the two $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ refer to distinct parts of an event. Similarly, the two $\Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ refer to distinct parts of an event. The execution \ref{fig:rendezvous with duration execution} captures this notion. Note that all arrows corresponding to $\HB{}$ are diagonal arrows.
\end{enumerate}

\input{figures/rendezvous_without_and_with_duration_executions.tex}

\section{Global Protocols} \label{sec:Global Protocols}
A global protocol is a specification of the events of parties, defined with global knowledge of what events all parties have.
For example, global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} specifies the events of parties $\party{A}$, $\party{B}$, and $\party{C}$.

\input{subequations/simple_global_protocol.tex}

The syntax of global protocols \ref{fig:global protocol syntax} is explained as follows:
\begin{description}
\item[\protect{\parbox[t]{\widthof{\boldmath\bfseries \text{$\guardP{\Ep{\Party}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party'}{i}}$}}}{$\transmit{\Party}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'}$ where \\ $\Party \neq \Party'$}}] This is a transmission, read as ``the transmission uniquely identified by $i$ specifies that $\Party$ sends a message to $\Party'$ over channel $\Channel$''.
  The condition $\Party \neq \Party'$ syntactically prohibits self-transmissions.
\item[$\guardP{\Ep{\Party}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party'}{i}}$] This is a guard, read as ``it remains to be proven that event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ happens before event $\Ep{\Party'}{i}$''. If a guard is proven, then the logical assertion $\Ep{\Party}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party'}{i}$ is known to be true. Further discussion of guards is deferred to section \ref{sec:Verifications, Implementations, and Guards}.
\item[$\emp$] The empty global protocol $\emp$ does nothing.
\item[$\GlobalProtocol \ssep \GlobalProtocol$] Global protocols may be sequentially composed by $\ssep$, such that one global protocol executes before the other.
\item[$\GlobalProtocol \asep \GlobalProtocol$] Global protocols may be concurrently composed by $\asep$, such that the two global protocols can execute at the same time.
  The concurrently composed global protocol does not impose any ordering between any event of the first global protocol and any event of the second global protocol.
\end{description}

This syntax is the syntax of session logic, but restricted to only transmissions, the empty protocol, sequential composition, and concurrent composition, as well as extended with guards.
Like Bocchi's session logic \parencite{Bocchi2012AMM}, our session logic is session types extended with logical assertions.
According to \textcite{10.1145/1328438.1328472}, ``session types model communications that often have a highly structured sequence of interactions, which as a whole form a natural unit of conversation. The structure of a conversation is abstracted as a session type through an intuitive syntax''.

We extend the usual session type syntax, by annotating transmissions with unique positive indexes.
Indexes are annotated by traversing the global protocol from left to right, and labelling transmissions with consecutive indexes starting from $1$.
For example, in global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol}, $\transmit{\party{A}}{\Channel}{1}{\party{B}}$ has index $1$, and $\transmit{\party{B}}{\Channel}{2}{\party{C}}$ has index $2$.
Transmission indexes are defined so that we can refer to the events of a transmission.
For example, global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} has the events $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$, $\Ep{\party{B}}{1}$, $\Ep{\party{B}}{2}$, and $\Ep{\party{C}}{2}$.

Our session logic has CSL as the underlying logic of its logical assertions.
Therefore, similar to \citeauthor{Bocchi2012AMM}'s session logic, our logical assertions can refer to the local state of each goroutine.
Moreover, separation logic allows, by the frame rule, a parallel decomposition that relates local computation of parallel programs to local computations of its components \parencite{BROOKES2007227}.

Other works that define session logics are \textcite{oortwijn2019abstractions} and \textcite{craciun2015towards}.
In both works, the session type and the logical assertions are able to share information.
For example, \textcite{oortwijn2019abstractions} defines a program annotation $\textbf{query } \text{b}$ that allows the logical assertion to assume a Boolean property $\text{b}$, which is proven to hold by process-algebraic analysis on the session type.

The syntax of global protocols include concurrent composition.
We explained that the two global protocols can execute at the same time.
This coincides with the usual notions of concurrent composition \parencites{gischer1988pomsets}{Hoare2009ConcurrentKA}, where composed parts execute concurrently.
However, we need to consider that in Go, parties must execute sequentially.
Therefore, there are cases where the concurrently composed global protocol imposes an ordering between some events of the first global protocol and some events of the second global protocol.

Consider the global protocol $\transmit{\party{A}}{\channel{c}{2}}{1}{\party{B}} \asep \transmit{\party{C}}{\channel{d}{2}}{2}{\party{A}}$.
In implementation \ref{lst:global protocol implementation concurrent}, the party $\party{A}$ that implements all of $\party{A}$'s events can order $\party{A}$'s send before $\party{A}$'s receive, as if the global protocol were sequentially composed instead of concurrently composed.
However, concurrent composition gives more freedom of implementation, in that it allows the party $\party{A}$ to instead order $\party{A}$'s receive before $\party{A}$'s send.
However, the party $\party{A}$ is not allowed to execute $\party{A}$'s concurrently with $\party{A}$'s receive.
In other words, parties are not allowed to spawn more concurrently executing parties.
Note that the \lstinline{main} goroutine is not a party, and therefore is allowed to spawn concurrently executing parties.
All concurrently executing parties must be determined in advance, and specified by the global protocol.

Other works \parencite[Section 4.4]{ng2016deadlock} similarly prohibit dynamic spawning of parties.

\input{lstlistings/global_protocol_implementation_concurrent.tex}

The syntax of global protocols syntactically prohibits self-transmissions with the condition $\Party \neq \Party'$, to avoid the possibility of deadlock.
Deadlock is possible when self-transmissions are allowed, in the case where the self-transmission of a goroutine $\Party$ occurs on an unbuffered channel.
$\Party$ deadlocks because goroutines execute sequentially, so that there is never an overlap between the durations of the send and the receive of the self-transmission.
The rendezvous never happens.

Other works \parencite{DY2013} have similar syntactic conditions that prohibit self-sent messages in session types.

We also prohibit self-transmissions caused by the semantics of the concurrent composition operator $\asep$, to once again avoid the possibility of deadlock.
We achieve this by imposing \citeauthor{costea2017session}'s well-formedness condition of nondeterministic global protocols \parencite[Definition 12]{costea2017session}, which we will not restate in this work.
However, we will restate their explanation of why a non-well-formed global protocol $\transmit{\party{A}}{\channel{c}{2}}{1}{\party{B}} \asep \transmit{\party{C}}{\channel{c}{2}}{2}{\party{A}}$ will deadlock.
Their explanation refers to implementation \ref{lst:non-well-formed global protocol implementation deadlocked}.
The goroutine $\party{A}$ that implements all of $\party{A}$'s events in the global protocol is allowed to order $\party{A}$'s receive before $\party{A}$'s send, because the global protocol is non-well-formed, and concurrent composition does not fix the order of these events.
If a program that implements goroutine $\party{A}$ this way executes such that $\party{B}$ actually receives data from $\party{C}$'s send, then $\party{A}$'s receive will block forever, since no sends will ever execute ($\party{A}$'s receive must finish executing before $\party{A}$'s send can execute).

\input{lstlistings/non-well-formed_global_protocol_implementation_deadlocked.tex}

Despite these syntactic and semantic prohibitions, we do not sacrifice expressiveness of our session logic, because it is still possible for parties to self-transmit.
For example, the global protocol $\transmit{\party{A}}{\Channel}{1}{\party{B}} \ssep \transmit{\party{B}}{\Channel}{2}{\party{A}}$, where all transmissions transmit the same message, simulates a self-transmission of party $\party{A}$.

\subsection{Partial Order Representation and Races}
Global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} specifies that party $\party{B}$'s events must happen in the order given by party $\party{B}$'s program order, because the global protocol orders $\party{B}$'s events with the $\HB{}$ relation such that $\party{B}$'s receive happens-before $\party{B}$'s send.
The global protocol also specifies that party $\party{B}$ \textit{should} receive data from party $\party{A}$, and party $\party{C}$ \textit{should} receive data from party $\party{B}$, because the global protocol orders events with the $\CB{}$ relation in that way.

We said $\party{B}$ \textit{should} (and not \textit{must}) receive data from $\party{A}$, where \textit{should} receive data means the protocol expects that $\party{B}$ receives data from $\party{A}$, and \textit{must} receive data means there is no execution where $\party{B}$ does not receive data from $\party{A}$.
The reason for this distinction between \textit{should} and \textit{must} is: an execution of the global protocol may be such that $\party{B}$ does not receive data from $\party{A}$, as in figure \ref{fig:simple global protocol sequential execution with races}.\footnote{The figure actually shows a sequential execution, but a sequential execution is a special kind of execution.}

To model the notion of ``\textit{should} receive data'', we define a communicates-before order $\CB{}$ as a set of triples $(\E{S}, \Channel, \E{R})$, where the global protocol expects $\E{R}$ to receive data from $\E{S}$ on channel $\Channel$, as expressed by the global subprotocol $\transmit{\E{S}}{\Channel}{i}{\E{R}}$.
Despite this expectation that $\E{R}$ receives data from $\E{S}$, an execution could have $\E{R}$ receive data from a different send, or have $\E{R}$ not receive any data at all. We call such deviations from the global protocol ``races''.
We consider an execution with races to be buggy, and we also consider the program that performed this execution to be buggy.
If a global protocol may be satisfied by an implementation which may execute with races, then we call this a ``global protocol with races''.
Otherwise, we call this a ``race-free global protocol''.
Unlike buggy executions with races, we do not consider a global protocol with races to be buggy, because the global protocol is the ultimate source of truth.
Therefore, we assume that the global protocol designer intended for the global protocol to have races.

A race-free global protocol always has race-free executions.
One possible race-free execution is the execution that replaces each $\E{S} \CB{\Channel} \E{R}$ with $\E{S} \HB{\Channel} \E{R}$, such that $\E{R}$ \textit{must} receive data from $\E{S}$.

We \textit{could} avoid defining $\CB{}$ by using $\E{S} \HB{\Channel} \E{R}$ for each $\E{S} \CB{\Channel} \E{R}$ in global protocols, with the provision that: under the context of global protocols, all $\E{S} \HB{\Channel} \E{R}$ actually means is that the receiver \textit{should} receive data. The problem with this is: under the context of executions, $\E{S} \HB{} \E{R}$ still means the receiver \textit{must} receive data. This double meaning of $\HB{}$ is potentially confusing. Introducing the $\CB{}$ relation avoids this confusion.

A global protocol can be represented with a partial order, over a set containing both the starts and the completions of events, by transforming the global protocol according to the following transformation:

\begin{description}[labelwidth=0pt]

\item[$\CB{\Channel}$ generation:] Each $\transmit{\Party}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'}$ is transformed into $\Ep{\Party}{i} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\Party'}{i}$.
  For example, global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} generates $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ and $\Ep{\party{B}}{2} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}$.

\item[$\HB{}$ generation:]
  For any two transmissions ordered by sequential composition,\footnote{A formal definition of whether two transmissions are ordered by sequential composition is given by \citeauthor{costea2017session} \parencite[Definition 8]{costea2017session}. For transmissions $\transmit{\Party}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'}$ and $\transmit{\Party''}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'''}$, suppose that these transmissions are composed with many global subprotocols, like in the global protocol $(\transmit{\Party}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'} \asep \GlobalProtocol) \ssep (\GlobalProtocol' \asep \transmit{\Party''}{\Channel}{i}{\Party''')}$, where $\GlobalProtocol$ and $\GlobalProtocol'$ are global subprotocols. The formal definition still sequentially orders these transmissions, so that even these arbitrarily nested transmissions generate $\HB{}$ if party equality holds.\label{foot:formal two transmissions ordered sequentially}} such that $\transmit{\Party}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'}$ occurs before $\transmit{\Party''}{\Channel}{i}{\Party'''}$:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item If $\Party = \Party''$, then $\Ep{\Party}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{i}$.
  \item If $\Party = \Party'''$, then $\Ep{\Party}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party'''}{i}$.
  \item If $\Party' = \Party''$, then $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{i}$.
  \item If $\Party' = \Party'''$, then $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party'''}{i}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  where party equality is defined in the obvious way, such that for example $\text{party } \party{A} = \text{party } \party{A}$.
  These generated $\HB{}$ elements are the program order of the respective parties.
  This $\HB{}$ ordering is similar to \citeauthor{10.1145/1328438.1328472}'s prefix ordering \parencite[Definition 3.3]{10.1145/1328438.1328472} for asynchronous communications, which imposes sequencing only on the actions of the same participant in ordered prefixes.

  As an example of generated $\HB{}$ elements, the global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} generates $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$.
\end{description}

As an example of this transformation, we represent the global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} with a partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order}.
The partial order specifies the same things that the global protocol specifies.

The partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order} is drawn as a sequence diagram \ref{fig:simple global protocol}.
A solid arrow from $\E{}$ to $\E{'}$ denotes $\E{} \HB{} \E{'}$, and a dotted arrow from $\E{}$ to $\E{'}$ denotes $\E{} \CB{\Channel} \E{'}$. Dotted arrows are labelled with the channel on which communication happens.
The vertical arrow $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$ is given by $\party{B}$'s program order.

Global protocols are defined up to party renaming, where if a party is replaced with another party, it is replaced everywhere in that global protocol.
For example, the global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol} with $\party{B}$ renamed to $\party{D}$ is global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol party renamed}.

\input{subequations/simple_global_protocol_party_renamed.tex}

which is defined to be the same as the global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol}.

\subsection{Indistinguishability of Global Protocols and Partial Orders}
We can change which party each event in the partial order belongs to. The partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order} is the same as the partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order different party}, but with event $\Ep{\party{B}}{2}$ renamed to event $\Ep{\party{D}}{2}$ everywhere. Note that we are renaming events, but not renaming parties.

\input{subequations/simple_global_protocol_equivalence_class.tex}

An equivalence class of partial orders contains partial orders with the same structure, but different party information.
Therefore, an equivalence class of partial orders is the equivalent partial order that does not contain party information.
For example, both \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order} and \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order different party} are in the equivalence class \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order no party}:

\input{subequations/simple_global_protocol_partial_order_no_party.tex}

We can define the inverse transformation from a partial order back to the global protocol.
Therefore, each equivalence class of partial orders corresponds to their equivalence class of global protocols.
For example, the equivalence class \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order no party} corresponds to the set containing global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol} (corresponding to the partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order}), global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol with guards} (corresponding to the partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order different party}), and possibly other global protocols.
Therefore, global protocols \ref{fig:simple global protocol} and \ref{fig:simple global protocol with guards} are equal up to the equivalence relation that defines these equivalence classes.

The global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol with guards} has a guard.
In general, a global protocol may have guards.
Recall that the partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order different party} that corresponds to the global protocol, is the same as partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order}, but with event $\Ep{\party{B}}{2}$ renamed to event $\Ep{\party{D}}{2}$ everywhere.
In partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order}, the order $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$ is given by program order of $\party{B}$.
In partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order different party}, event $\Ep{\party{B}}{2}$ has been renamed to $\Ep{\party{D}}{2}$, so that the order $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$ no longer exists, and is no longer given by program order of $\party{B}$.
The guard $\guardP{\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{D}}{2}}$ in the global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol with guards} allows our verification framework to distinguish between the implementations that guarantee the ordering $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{D}}{2}$, and the implementations that do not guarantee the ordering.
Our framework verifies with success only the implementations that guarantee the ordering $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{D}}{2}$.
Further discussion on proving guards is deferred to section \ref{sec:Verifications, Implementations, and Guards}.

Not all partial orders correspond to a global protocol.
For example, the partial order $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\party{B}}{1} \land \Ep{\party{A}}{2} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\party{B}}{2} \land \Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{A}}{2}$ does not correspond to a global protocol.
The $\HB{}$ element $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{A}}{2}$ indicates that global protocol consists of sequentially composed transmissions $\transmit{\party{A}}{\Channel}{1}{\party{B}} \ssep \transmit{\party{A}}{\Channel}{2}{\party{B}}$, but then sequential composition indicates that the $\HB{}$ order must also have the element $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$, and yet the partial order does not have this element.
The inverse transformation from a partial order back to a global protocol maps these partial orders that do not correspond to a global protocol, to the empty set.

In this work, we only discuss partial orders that correspond to a global protocol.
Due to this correspondence, in this work, we do not distinguish between a global protocol and its partial order.
For example, in the figure \ref{fig:simple global protocol}, the partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order} is written as a global protocol, and shown as a sequence diagram.

\section{Sequential Executions} \label{sec:Sequential Executions}
A sequential execution is a special kind of execution.

A sequential execution that refines a global protocol is a linear order, ordered only by the $\HB{}$ relation, on both the starts and the completions of events, for all events.
The linear order of a sequential execution that refines a global protocol is a linearization with the same underlying set of events as the set of events in the global protocol.
The linearization contains the global protocol's $\HB{}$ order, and maybe also contains some $\HB{\Channel}$ elements between sends and receives not in the global protocol, where each added $\HB{\Channel}$ can have different $\Channel$.
In a sequential execution, all events must be atomic, so that there is no event between the start and the completion of an event.
Each added $\E{S} \HB{\Channel} \E{R}$ for some $\Channel$ means the receive $\E{R}$ actually receives data from send $\E{S}$ on channel $\Channel$, and the completion of $\E{S}$ happens-before the start of $\E{R}$.
Each added $\E{} \HB{} \E{'}$ means the sequential execution executes in such a way that the completion of $\E{}$ happens-before the start of $\E{'}$.

Note that the linear order of a sequential execution does not include elements from the $\CB{}$ order of the global protocol: intuitively, a sequential execution does not care about how sends are specified to communicate with receives, it only cares about which receives actually receives data from certain sends (as given by $\HB{}$).

We are motivated to define sequential executions, because in most cases, sequential executions are easier to discuss about than concurrent executions.
Sequential execution events are atomic, so that we can define sequential execution events to be instantaneous without duration.
Therefore, when discussing sequential executions, we do not need to mention the start or completion of a sequential execution event.
We only need to mention the sequential execution event as a whole.
As another consequence, sequence diagrams of sequential executions become more concise.
For the rest of this work, the only executions we will consider are sequential executions with atomic events, except for when we must consider concurrent executions, or except for when we are citing another work.

A sequential execution simulates a concurrent execution.
We are allowed to represent a concurrent execution with a sequential execution, because this is similar to how true concurrency semantics and interleaved concurrency semantics are indistinguishable for process calculi.
Interleaved concurrency semantics simulates true concurrency semantics by arriving at the same conclusion in two reductions instead of one reduction. Process calculi do not distinguish the proof of a conclusion by the number of reductions.

A true concurrency rule that reduces process $P$ to process $P'$ and process $Q$ to process $Q'$:

$$\Rule{P \rightarrow P' \qquad Q \rightarrow Q'}{P \parallel Q  \rightarrow  P' \parallel Q'}$$

can be simulated by applying the two interleaved concurrency rules in sequence:

\begin{align*}
  \Rule{P \rightarrow P'}{P \parallel Q  \rightarrow  P' \parallel Q} & & \Rule{Q \rightarrow Q'}{P' \parallel Q  \rightarrow  P' \parallel Q'}
\end{align*}

Similarly, the sequential semantics for any two events that concurrently access a shared channel (send and send, send and receive, receive and send, receive and receive) is a linearization of this concurrent access, with the condition that no other events happen in-between these two events.
Intuitively, this means the two linearized concurrent events are regarded by all other events to happen at nearly the same time.
This simulates that the two linearized concurrent events happen at the same time.

However, there is one case where a sequential execution does not simulate a concurrent execution.
If $\E{S}$ and $\E{R}$ are events of a rendezvous, then the start of $\E{R}$ happens-before the completion of $\E{S}$, and by asymmetry of $\HB{}$, the completion of $\E{S}$ cannot happen-before the start of $\E{R}$.
There is a conflict between the definitions of rendezvous and sequential execution, because the completion of $\E{S}$ cannot happen-before the start of $\E{R}$, yet if we apply the definition of a sequential execution to a rendezvous, then the completion of $\E{S}$ must happen-before the start of $\E{R}$.
We resolve this case of conflict in the next section, so that by the end of that section, it should be clear that a sequential execution simulates a concurrent execution.

\subsection{Legal Sequential Executions}
Not all sequential executions are legal. For example, the global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol} can never execute in the way given by the sequential execution \ref{fig:simple global protocol sequential execution with races illegal}.
This is because the sequential execution orders the receives such that $\Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ happens-before $\Ep{\party{C}}{2}$, and also says that the first send $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ sends data to the second receive $\Ep{\party{C}}{2}$.
However, by rule \eqref{eq:send before receive}, the first send $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ must send data to the first receive $\Ep{\party{B}}{1}$, not to the second receive.
This sequential execution is illegal because it violates rule \eqref{eq:send before receive}.

Using this observation, we can determine whether any given sequential execution is illegal.
\begin{lemma}
  There is an algorithm to determine whether any given sequential execution is illegal.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  Since the sequential execution linearizes concurrent sends, our verification knows which send the $i^{th}$ send is, and since the sequential execution linearizes concurrent receives, our verification knows which receive the $i^{th}$ receive is.
  Then, the rules \eqref{eq:send before receive} and \eqref{eq:receive before send} give a happens-before order, which we add to our $\HB{}$ order.
  If the resulting $\HB{}$ order has a cycle, then the sequential execution is illegal.
\end{proof}

In this work, we consider only legal sequential executions.

\input{figures/simple_global_protocol_sequential_execution_with_races_illegal.tex}

\subsection{Sequential Executions of Rendezvous}
Sequential executions must have atomic events, but this conflicts with the fact that the send and receive of a rendezvous must happen at the same time.
We resolve this conflict by redefining the sequential execution of a rendezvous.
A sequential execution must respect the semantics of a rendezvous:
\input{subequations/rendezvous_semantics.tex}
Semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics transmit} is self-evident. Semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics send blocks} is given by rule \eqref{eq:send before receive}, while semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics receive blocks} is given by rule \eqref{eq:receive before send}.
Therefore, although atomic events have no notion of the ``start'' of an event or the ``completion'' of an event, these notions are still present in the memory model rules, and these (explicit) rules are now the (implicit) semantics that the sequential execution must respect.
In the following discussion about semantics, we show sequential executions such that its events are events with duration with a start and completion, because the discussion of semantics will mention the notions of ``start'' and ``completion''.

To respect semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics transmit}, we have the rendezvous sequential execution \ref{fig:rendezvous sequential execution with events with duration} order the send before the receive: data has to be in-flight before it can be received.\footnote{We believe that it is also possible to respect semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics transmit} if the sequential execution instead orders receive before send. However, we find this tougher to explain.} In other words, the sequential execution simulates that the data is stored in a buffered channel with capacity $1$.

The sequential execution \ref{fig:rendezvous sequential execution with events with duration} also respects semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics receive blocks} (shown by the blue arrow), but does not respect semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics send blocks} (shown by the red arrow), because the send happens-before the receive (shown by the black arrow); the send does not wait for the receive to start.

Another way of noticing that the sequential execution \ref{fig:rendezvous sequential execution with events with duration} does not respect semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics send blocks} is, the sequential execution has a cycle formed by the red arrow and the black arrow, violating the assymetry condition of $\HB{}$.

To resolve this, we need to ensure the sequential execution satisfies some semantic conditions in figure \ref{fig:semantic conditions} that simulate the semantics \eqref{eq:sequential execution rendezvous semantics send blocks}.
We do not need to consider semantic conditions \eqref{eq:aft-recvs are aft-sends} and \eqref{eq:bef-sends are before-recvs}, because these are already satisfied by ordering the send before the receive.\footnote{If the rendezvous sequential execution instead ordered the receive before the send, then we would require the sequential execution to satisfy these other two semantic conditions.}
The sequential execution must satisfy condition \eqref{eq:bef-recvs are before-sends} such that no event of the sender happens-between the send and the receive, and the sequential execution must satisfy condition \eqref{eq:aft-sends are aft-recvs} such that no event of the receiver happens-between the send and the receive.

\input{figures/semantic_conditions.tex}

The semantic conditions \ref{fig:semantic conditions} must satisfy the requirement \ref{req:there are no other events on an unbuffered channel}, because if there is another receive $\E{R'}$ that happens concurrently with the receive $\E{R}$, then it is possible for a sequential execution to rendezvous $\E{R'}$ with $\E{S}$ instead.
In other words, in the sequential execution, we no longer have $\E{S} \HB{\channel{c}{0}} \E{R}$, therefore the conclusions of each semantic condition may no longer hold.

\begin{req} \label{req:there are no other events on an unbuffered channel}
  $\E{S}$ and $\E{R}$ are the only events occurring on channel $\channel{c}{0}$.
\end{req}

The semantic conditions \ref{fig:semantic conditions} and the requirement together ensure that no event of the global protocol happens-between the send and the receive.
A sequential execution with atomic events that satisfies the semantics of rendezvous is \ref{fig:rendezvous sequential execution with atomic events}.

To conclude the section, a concurrent execution of a rendezvous can be simulated as a sequential execution, if the sequential execution satisfies certain semantic conditions.
For the rest of the paper, any sequential execution of a rendezvous satisfies the semantic conditions.
We have only considered rendezvous, but similar considerations of semantics can be made for e.g. global protocols that communicate over buffered channels.

\subsection{Race-free Sequential Executions} \label{sec:Race-free Sequential Executions}
As another example of a sequential execution, global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol} can have the sequential execution \ref{fig:simple global protocol sequential execution race-free}.
This sequential execution is race-free, because:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Each receiver receives data from some sender.
\item Each receiver receives data from the correct sender, as specified by the global protocol.
\end{enumerate}
Intuitively, a race-free sequential execution communicates according to the global protocol.

The global protocol may also have a sequential execution with races \ref{fig:simple global protocol sequential execution with races}, such that $\party{C}$ receives data from $\party{A}$ instead of $\party{B}$ receiving data from $\party{A}$, and $\party{B}$ does not receive any data at all.

Combining these observations, we can conjecture this:
\begin{conj}
If the linear order of a sequential execution is a linearization of the order that is the union of the $\HB{}$ order of the global protocol \textit{and the $\CB{}$ order of the global protocol}, then the sequential execution is race-free. Otherwise, the sequential execution has races. \label{conj:sequential execution global protocol equivalence has races conjecture}
\end{conj}
Note that by the definition in section \ref{sec:Sequential Executions}, a sequential execution is already a linearization of the $\HB{}$ order of the global protocol.
Conjecture \ref{conj:sequential execution global protocol equivalence has races conjecture} says that if the linear order of the sequential execution furthermore contains the $\CB{}$ order of the global protocol, then the sequential execution is race-free.
Intuitively, a race-free sequential execution executes communications according to the global protocol.

\section{Verifications, Implementations, and Guards} \label{sec:Verifications, Implementations, and Guards}
We have described in section \ref{sec:Program Order, Events, Sequential Consistency, and Parties} how events are defined from a line of code in programs, and we use events to define global protocols in section \ref{sec:Global Protocols}.
We now describe how to verify if a given program, which is called an ``implementation'', satisfies a given global protocol.
We consider only verifications of implementations.

We now define guards.
A guard $\guardP{\Psi}$ is a proof obligation of proposition $\Psi$.
In other words, a guard is an abstraction over how proposition $\Psi$ is proven.
Only protocols may have guards.
If a guard is proven, then the protocol knows that proposition $\Psi$ is true.
Only verifications may prove guards.
A verification proves a guard $\guardP{\Psi}$ only if the verification can deduce via some proof rules that $\Psi$ is true.
An implementation satisfies a global protocol only if the implementation communicates according to the global protocol, and if the verification proves all the guards in the global protocol.

In global protocols, guards are sequentially composed like so: $\GlobalProtocol \ssep \guardP{\Psi} \ssep \GlobalProtocol'$, where $\GlobalProtocol$ is the global protocol before the guard, and $\GlobalProtocol'$ is the global protocol after the guard.
An implementation is verified for satisfaction of the global protocol.
We now describe each part of such a verification.
\begin{description}
\item[$\GlobalProtocol$] If $\GlobalProtocol$ does not contain another $\guardP{\Psi}$, then verification of $\GlobalProtocol$ proceeds without knowing whether $\Psi$ is true.
  This is because the sequential composition operator $\ssep$ requires that the verification verifies the global protocol $\GlobalProtocol$ before $\Psi$ is proven.
  If the implementation fails to satisfy $\GlobalProtocol$, then the verification terminates with failure.
  Otherwise, the verification continues, checking if the next part of the implementation satisfies the next part of the global protocol.
\item[$\guardP{\Psi}$]
  If the verification fails to prove the guard, then the verification terminates with failure.
  Otherwise, the verification continues, checking if the next part of the implementation satisfies the next part of the global protocol.
\item[$\GlobalProtocol'$] If verification reaches this part of the global protocol, then verification of the implementation against $\GlobalProtocol'$ proceeds with the knowledge that $\Psi$ is true.
  This is because $\guardP{\Psi}$ was already proven true by the verification, and the sequential composition operator $\ssep$ requires that the verification prove $\Psi$ before the rest of the global protocol $\GlobalProtocol'$ is verified.
\end{description}
For example, the global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol with guards} has a global protocol $\transmit{\party{A}}{\Channel}{1}{\party{B}}$ before the guard, the guard $\guardP{\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{D}}{2}}$, and a global protocol $\transmit{\party{D}}{\Channel}{2}{\party{C}}$ after the guard.

\subsection{Guards of $\HB{}$}
In this work, we consider only guards $\guardP{\Psi}$ where $\Psi$ is an assertion that an element is in $\HB{}$.
These guards have the form $\guardP{\E{} \HB{} \E{'}}$.
A verification proves $\guardP{\E{} \HB{} \E{'}}$ only if the verification proves that $\E{} \HB{} \E{'}$ indeed exists in $\HB{}$, which in turn only occurs if the implementation is implemented in a certain way.

There are at least two ways that an implementation can make a verification prove guards $\guardP{\E{} \HB{} \E{'}}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The program order of a party shows that $\guardP{\E{} \HB{} \E{'}}$ is true, where $\E{}$ and $\E{'}$ are events of the same party
\item Synchronization. Although there are many synchronization primitives in Go, for the rest of this work we will only consider synchronization by sending and receiving on an unbuffered channel.
\end{enumerate}
For example, the guard $\guardP{\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{D}}{2}}$ in the global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol with guards} may be proved through synchronizations by an implementation.

\subsection{Transforming Global Protocols with Races into Race-free Global Protocols} \label{sec:Transforming Global Protocols with Races into Race-free Global Protocols}
Guards can be used to prove arbitrary properties.
In this section, we use guards to prove that a global protocol is FIFO race-free.

A global protocol with races can be transformed into a FIFO race-free global protocol.
We first descriptively specify the transformation as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Linearly order sends by $\HB{}$, so that there is only one way data can be written to the channel. We denote the linear order on sends by $<_S$. The linear order $<_S$ must not violate the program order of any party. The proof that the sends are linearly ordered is deferred as guards.
\item Ensure that channels are FIFO, so that data written to the channel is read in the same order from the channel. Note that FIFO channels do not fix the order of sends or receives.
\item Linearly order receives by $\HB{}$, so that there is only one way data can be read from the channel. We denote the linear order on receives by $<_R$. The linear order $<_R$ must not violate the program order of any party. The proof that the receives are linearly ordered is deferred as guards.
\end{enumerate}

Furthermore, the sending order is required to be equivalent to the receiving order. This requirement is rephrased as follows.
Recall that given a global protocol, for each transmission $\transmit{\E{S}}{\Channel}{i}{\E{R}}$ in that global protocol, $\CB{\Channel}$ relates its sender $\E{S}$ to its receiver $\E{R}$.
We define the left operation $\receiveOfSendP{\E{S}} = \E{R}$.
The requirement is that $\receiveOfSendP{\cdot}$ is order-preserving, given by rule \eqref{eq:CB is isotone}.

\input{subequations/cb_is_isotone.tex}

This way of ensuring that access to the endpoint of a shared channel is linear is similar to the statement ``Programs that modify data being simultaneously accessed by multiple goroutines must serialize such access.'' \parencite{go/ref/mem}, as well as the approach of \parencite{adve1991detecting} to avoid data races for sequentially consistent executions.

We now operationally specify the transformation as follows.
Given a global protocol, e.g. global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol}, do the following for each pair of transmissions ordered by the $\ssep$ operator.\footnote{Recall from footnote \ref{foot:formal two transmissions ordered sequentially} that the formal definition of sequential order allows arbitrarily nested transmissions to still be sequentially ordered.}
If a pair of transmissions are on the same channel, e.g. $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\party{B}}{1} \land \Ep{\party{B}}{2} \CB{\Channel} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}$ on channel $\Channel$ in partial order \eqref{eq:simple global protocol partial order}, then we prove that the send of the first transmission happens-before the send of the second transmission, e.g. $\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}$, and we prove that the receive of the first transmission happens-before the receive of the second transmission, e.g. $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}$.
The proofs of these are abstracted as guards, e.g. $\guardP{\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}}$, and $\guardP{\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}}$.
The guards are inserted by sequential composition into the global protocol between the pair of transmissions.
The guards are inserted between the pair of transmissions, so that verification of the implementation proceeds to the second transmission only if the verification can show that the pair of transmissions alone is FIFO race-free (Intuitively, under the context of verifying FIFO race-freedom, there is no point in verifying a transmission that races. This is because if the verification already knows that the transmission will race, then the verification should immediately terminate with failure). Then, the guards are proved by verification of an implementation, e.g. implementation \ref{lst:simple global protocol guarded implementation}.
If the guards of all such pairs of transmissions are proven by verification, then verification would have shown that $\receiveOfSendP{\cdot}$ is order-preserving for the entirety of the global protocol, and therefore shown that the global protocol is FIFO race-free.

If the global protocol designer deems the global protocol with races \ref{fig:simple global protocol} to be a design flaw, then the designer can use our transformation to automatically obtain a FIFO race-free global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol guarded}.

\input{figures/simple_global_protocol_guarded.tex}

The global protocol designer may insert arbitrary guards into a global protocol.
Despite this, $\HB{}$ remains a strict partial order.
It is impossible to prove that $\HB{}$ elements exist such that $\HB{}$ is not a strict partial order.
For example, $\guardP{\Ep{\party{C}}{2} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}}$ may be inserted into global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol guarded} to get global protocol \eqref{eq:simple global protocol guarded cycle}.

\input{subequations/simple_global_protocol_guarded_cycle.tex}

This new global protocol has the cycle consisting of two elements, $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}$ and $\Ep{\party{C}}{2} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}$.
By transitivity, we have $\Ep{\party{B}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{1}$ and $\Ep{\party{C}}{2} \HB{} \Ep{\party{C}}{2}$, violating asymmetry.
Such global protocols with cycles are called ``deadlocked global protocols'', because all implementations of such global protocols must deadlock, and all verifications must fail to prove some guard.

\subsection{Concurrent Executions and Order between Sends and Receives} \label{sec:Concurrent Executions and Order between Sends and Receives}
A race-free global protocol has linearized concurrent sends and linearized concurrent receives.
However, there is still more than one way to linearize the events consisting of both sends and receives.
For example, the global protocol \ref{fig:send receive rules global protocol} has three concurrent sends and three concurrent receives on a channel $\channel{c}{2}$ with buffer capacity $2$.
The following sequential executions of sends and receives of the global protocol are possible:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Two sends, then one receive, then one send, then two receives.
\item One send, then one receive, then two sends, then two receives.
\end{enumerate}
Instead of considering each possible sequential execution of sends and receives, we can consider only the concurrent execution with a partial $\HB{}$ order that subsumes all these sequential executions.
This is simply the $\HB{}$ given by the rules \eqref{eq:send before receive} and \eqref{eq:receive before send}.
The resulting $\HB{}$ order is shown in a concurrent execution \ref{fig:send receive rules happens-before}.
This figure can be made more tidy, as in figure \ref{fig:send receive rules happens-before tidy}.

Note that although this execution is concurrent, all sequential executions subsumed by this concurrent execution are race-free by conjecture \ref{conj:sequential execution global protocol equivalence has races conjecture}, therefore we also consider this concurrent execution to be race-free.

In previous sections, we have drawn figures that show the rules \eqref{eq:send before receive} and \eqref{eq:receive before send}, but those figures had either buffers of capacity $0$, or buffers of unspecified capacity.
There, the red arrows that correspond to $\HB{}$ elements given by rule \eqref{eq:receive before send} either point the $i^{th}$ receive to the $i^{th}$ send, or the red arrows do not exist at all.
This is the first time we draw figures that have a specific positive buffer capacity.
The red arrows in these figures showcase how the buffer capacity $k$ in rule \eqref{eq:receive before send} manifests itself in a $\HB{}$ partial order.

We emphasize that only verifications can prove that $\HB{}$ elements exist, and global protocols cannot prove that $\HB{}$ elements exist.
We also emphasize that this new global protocol is not a part of our verification framework. This new global protocol is described only for easier understanding.

The new global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol race-free} is the same as the old global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol guarded}, but with a transmission $\Ep{\party{A}}{1.3} \CB{\channel{d}{0}} \Ep{\party{B}}{1.3}$ on channel $\channel{d}{0}$ inserted after event $\Ep{\party{A}}{1}$ and before event $\Ep{\party{B}}{2}$.
We show that the verification of the implementation that corresponds to this new protocol proves the guard $\guardP{\Ep{\party{A}}{1} \HB{} \Ep{\party{B}}{2}}$ in the old global protocol.

\subsection{Projections}
In this section, we show how to obtain local views of a given global protocol.
We do so by defining two projection functions to obtain ``per-party protocols'', and ``per-endpoint protocols''.
In a party, all channels actually refer to the channel endpoint that the party communicates on.
The resulting projected protocols guide the verification of an implementation.
We focus on applying our framework to verify that a Go program is FIFO race-free.

A given implementation is verified as follows.
A given global protocol is projected onto each party of the global protocol, to get per-party protocols.
Then, each party of the implementation is verified against the corresponding per-party protocol.
Each party of the implementation satisfies its corresponding per-party protocol only if its verification succeeds.
An implementation satisfies the global protocol only if all parties of the implementation satisfies their corresponding per-party protocol.

The syntax of per-party protocols \ref{fig:per-party protocol syntax} is somewhat familiar. We now explain the unfamiliar syntax:
\begin{description}
\item[$\Ep{\Party}{i} \CB{\Channel}$] As part of transmission $i$, party $\Party$ sends on endpoint $\Channel$.
\item[$\CB{\Channel} \Ep{\Party}{i}$] As part of transmission $i$, party $\Party$ receives on endpoint $\Channel$.
\item[$\guardP{\channel{d}{\anything}, \Ep{\Party}{i}}$] Endpoint $\channel{d}{\anything}$ has the burden of proving proposition $\Ep{\Party}{i}$.
  We added the endpoint parameter $\channel{d}{\anything}$ to guards so that we can project guards onto endpoints to obtain per-endpoint guards.
  The proposition in this guard is an event.
  The proposition is proved only if the verification of party $\Party$ knows that the event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ already happened.
\end{description}
Concurrent composition $\asep$ is not defined in the syntax of per-party protocols, because a party is a goroutine that executes sequentially.

We do not use the familiar session type syntax of sends $\Channel!$ and receives $\Channel?$, because we want projection to preserve information about which event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ occurs in the party.

Projection of a global protocol onto party $\Party$ is the function $\projectOntoP{\cdot}{\Party}$ in figure \ref{fig:global to per-party projection}.
If a transmission $\transmit{\Party'}{\Channel}{i}{\Party''}$ is projected onto party $\Party'$, then the per-party protocol is the send $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \CB{\Channel}$.
If the transmission is instead projected onto party $\Party''$, then the per-party protocol is the receive $\CB{\Channel} \Ep{\Party''}{i}$.
Projection preserves inaction $\emp$.
Projection is defined recursively on sequentially composed and concurrently composed global protocols.

We give special attention to how projection is defined on guards $\guardP{\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$.
Intuitively, projection on a guard inserts a new rendezvous between the two events ordered by $\HB{}$ in the guard, like how two rendezvous were inserted into the old global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol guarded} to obtain the new global protocol \ref{fig:simple global protocol race-free}.
In reality, a new rendezvous is not actually inserted into the global protocol.
Rather, the send of the rendezvous is inserted into one per-party protocol, and the receive of the rendezvous is inserted into the other per-party protocol.

If a guard $\guardP{\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$ is projected onto party $\Party'$, then the per-party protocol is the sequential composition of the guard $\guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party'}{i}}$ and the send $\Ep{\Party'}{k} \CB{\channel{d}{0}}$, for some $\channel{d}{0}$ and some $k > i$.
If the guard is instead projected onto party $\Party''$, then the per-party protocol is the sequential composition of the receive $\CB{\channel{d}{0}} \Ep{\Party''}{h}$ and the guard $\guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$, for some $\channel{d}{0}$ and some $h < j$.
The send $\Ep{\Party'}{k} \CB{\channel{d}{0}}$ and the receive $\CB{\channel{d}{0}} \Ep{\Party''}{h}$ of the two projected protocols of a guard must rendezvous on the same unbuffered channel $\channel{d}{0}$.

The reason for defining projection on guards as such is as follows.
Consider an implementation that satisfies both guard-projected per-party protocols $\guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party'}{i}} \ssep \Ep{\Party'}{k} \CB{\channel{d}{0}}$ and $\CB{\channel{d}{0}} \Ep{\Party''}{h} \ssep \guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$.
Our verification approach verifies that the implementation indeed satisfies the guard $\guardP{\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$, by:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Knowing from $\guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party'}{i}} \ssep \Ep{\Party'}{k} \CB{\channel{d}{0}}$ that if verification reaches $\Ep{\Party'}{k} \CB{\channel{d}{0}}$, then verification of $\Ep{\Party'}{k} \CB{\channel{d}{0}}$ proceeds with the knowledge that $\Ep{\Party'}{i}$ has already happened.
  In other words, our verification knows that $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party'}{k}$.
\item Applying the semantic condition \eqref{eq:bef-sends are before-recvs} (instantiating $\E{}$ with $\Ep{\Party'}{i}$, $\E{S}$ with $\Ep{\Party'}{k}$, $\E{R}$ with $\Ep{\Party''}{h}$, and $\channel{c}{0}$ with $\channel{d}{0}$) to know that $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{h}$.
\item Knowing from $\CB{\channel{d}{0}} \Ep{\Party''}{h} \ssep \guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$ that if verification reaches $\guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$, then verification of $\guardP{\channel{d}{0}, \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$ proceeds with the knowledge that $\CB{\channel{d}{0}} \Ep{\Party''}{h}$ has already happened.
  In other words, our verification knows that $\Ep{\Party''}{h} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}$.
\end{enumerate}
All in all, if all per-party protocols are verified with success, then our verification could apply transitivity of $\HB{}$ on the known orders to know that $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}$, thus proving the guard $\guardP{\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}}$.
However, our verification does not need to actually apply transitivity of $\HB{}$, because to know that $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \HB{} \Ep{\Party''}{j}$, it is enough to ensure that both guard-projected per-party protocols are verified with success.
Therefore, applying transitivity of $\HB{}$ is not a verification step.

This limited definition of projection is enough to show FIFO race-freedom.

Although it is possible for implementations to be verified against per-party projections, we want finer-grained projections: we project the per-party protocol of party $A$ onto each endpoint $\Channel, \channel{d}{\anything}, \ldots$ used by $A$.

The syntax of per-endpoint protocols \ref{fig:per-endpoint protocol syntax} is somewhat familiar. We now explain the unfamiliar syntax:
\begin{description}
\item[$\Ep{\Party}{i} \CB{}$] A send event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ occurs on the endpoint.
\item[$\CB{} \Ep{\Party}{i}$] A receive event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ occurs on the endpoint.
\item[$\guardP{\Ep{\Party}{i}}$] The endpoint has the burden of proving proposition $\Ep{\Party}{i}$.
  The proposition is proved only if the verification of party $\Party$ knows that the event $\Ep{\Party}{i}$ already happened.
\end{description}
Concurrent composition $\asep$ is not defined in the syntax of per-endpoint protocols, because an endpoint sequentially executes the sends and receives that occur on it.

Projection of a per-party protocol onto endpoint $\Channel$ is the function $\projectOntoP{\cdot}{\Channel}$ in figure \ref{fig:per-party to per-endpoint projection}.
If a send $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \CB{\Channel}$ is projected onto endpoint $\Channel$, then the per-endpoint protocol is the send without endpoint information $\Ep{\Party'}{i} \CB{}$.
If a receive $\CB{\Channel} \Ep{\Party'}{i}$ is projected onto endpoint $\Channel$, then the per-endpoint protocol is the receive without endpoint information $\CB{} \Ep{\Party'}{i}$.
If a guard $\guardP{\channel{d}{\anything}, \Ep{\Party'}{i}}$ is projected onto endpoint $\channel{d}{\anything}$, then the per-endpoint protocol is the guard without endpoint information $\guardP{\Ep{\Party'}{i}}$.
Projection preserves inaction $\emp$.
Projection is defined recursively on sequentially composed and concurrently composed protocols.

Now that we have introduced the protocol syntax, we define structural congruence for these protocols.
Structural congruence is the smallest relation $\equiv$ on protocols that includes the relations in figure \ref{fig:protocol structural congruence}.
